**Derivation.** Rewrite $x^n+x=2^k+2$ as $(x-1)(x^{n-1}+x^{n-2}+\cdots+x+2)=2^k$. Both factors are powers of $2$. If $x$ is even then $x-1$ is an odd power of $2$, so $x-1=1$, i.e. $x=2$, contradicting $x>n\ge2$. Thus $x$ is odd, $x=2^a+1$ ($a\ge1$), and $S_n(x):=\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}x^i+2=2^b$ with $b\ge2$ (since $S_n(x)\ge x+2\ge5$).

Modulo $2$: $S_n(x)\equiv(n-1)+2=n+1$, so $n$ is odd. Modulo $4$: if $x\equiv3\pmod4$ then (as $n-1$ is even) the power-sum is $0\pmod4$, giving $S_n(x)\equiv2\pmod4$, impossible. Hence $x\equiv1\pmod4$ and $S_n(x)\equiv n+1\equiv0\pmod4$, so $n\equiv3\pmod4$.

Substituting $x=2^a+1$ into the original equation and expanding:
$$2^a\Bigl[(n+1)+\binom{n}{2}2^a+\cdots+2^{(n-1)a}\Bigr]=2^k.$$
If $a>v_2(n+1)$, the bracket has $2$-adic valuation $v_2(n+1)$ and odd part $>1$, so it is not a power of $2$. Thus $a\le v_2(n+1)$. Together with $x=2^a+1>n$ and $2^a\le 2^{v_2(n+1)}\le n+1$, we obtain $n<2^a+1\le n+2$, so $2^a+1\in\{n+1,n+2\}$. The case $2^a+1=n+1$ gives $n=2^a\not\equiv3\pmod4$; the case $2^a+1=n+2$ gives $n=2^a-1$, $x=2^a+1$.

For $a=2$: $(x,n)=(5,3)$, yielding $5^3+5=130=2^7+2$, so $k=7$. For $a\ge3$, the bracket equals $2^a[1+\binom{n}{2}+\cdots]$ where $1+\binom{2^a-1}{2}\equiv2\pmod4$, so the bracket is $2\pmod4$ and cannot be a power of $2$. Hence $(5,3,7)$ is the unique solution.
